He said: Mr. Speaker, when we had the opportunity of discussing the resolution which is preliminary to the present bill I endeavoured to give a full explanation of the purposes which the government had in mind in introducing these amendments to the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act. I do not think I can usefully add anything to the somewhat comprehensive explanation which I gave last week.
I think I might merely repeat that the principal need for the amendments to the act arises from the fact that the bridge carrying rail and road traffic over the south channel between Cornwall island and the mainland of the United States will have to be demolished in order to enable the passage of ships when the seaway is opened and that nearly all of the amendments that are contemplated by this bill are necessitated by measures that will have to be taken in consequence of the prospective removal of that bridge. I think the only one that is not directly related to that particular aspect of the matter is one concerning the disposition to be made of the proceeds realized from the disposition of property held in the name of the authority. There is one thing, however, I am a little at a loss to understand, and possibly the minister can clear it up at this stage. It is this. If in the future any other international bridges are to be built in the area under the jurisdiction of the St. Lawrence seaway authority, are these bridges going to be built by the seaway authority or by some other private or public authority?

The reason I inquire in this regard has to do with certain remarks made by the minister, at the bottom of the first column on page 3217 of Hansard. The minister said:
I would not like the committee to think for a moment that this is a departure from the main purpose of the St. Lawrence seaway authority which, as hon. members know, is to build a deep waterway from Montreal to lake Erie and not to go into the building of a series of bridges across the river, either in the international rapids section or anywhere else. If it had not been for this particular situation and the fact that the replacement of the bridge across the south channel necessitates an international bridge I do not think it would have been necessary to bring in this legislation.
I gather from those remarks of the minister that, apart from a particularized situation in the Cornwall area, where there is a big dam being built, the other reason the St. Lawrence seaway authority was going into this matter of constructing a bridge was that an international bridge was necessitated.
In 1952 a private bill went through this house to incorporate the Ogdensburg Bridge Company. Until July 2 of next year, this particular company, which was incorporated for the purpose of constructing an international bridge across the St. Lawrence river in the neighbourhood of Prescott, it would seem to me, might with the consent of the governor in council build this bridge. It might ask permission any time up to next July. If that is the case, I wish the minister would clarify the position if the Ogdensburg Bridge Company, which I point out is a private company, asked for permission to build such a bridge, whether or not, in the opinion of the minister, such permission would be granted or whether, since it is an international bridge-as the minister has pointed out-required to go across the St. Lawrence, it would probably be the seaway authority itself that would construct any such international bridge in this area, which at present is under the jurisdiction of the seaway authority.
I believe I have mentioned this matter on an earlier occasion in the resolution stage but, in view of the minister's remarks, I would be much obliged-and I am sure other members interested in this would be too- if the minister could tell us whether or not all international bridges in the area under the jurisdiction of the St. Lawrence seaway authority are going to be built by the authority or whether private or other public authorities will be building bridges in this area.

As I said the other day, the current lease actually ends on December 31, 1957, but in 1950 at a time when the bridge company was considering making some substantial expenditures on the property it had leased it arranged for a 25-year additional lease to run from December 31, 1957, so the expiry date is now December 31, 1982. This is one of these percentage leases and the New York Central or one of its subsidiaries receives rental based on the amount of revenues collected by the bridge company.
I am afraid I cannot tell my hon. friend very much about the bridge company itself. The shares are not listed and I believe they are privately held. It is hoped that it will be possible to work out with the bridge company an arrangement for the purchase of its shares or the purchase of its relevant assets so as to avoid both the cost and delay involved in a long examination of the amount of damages that would be suffered by the corporation itself.
If you expropriated only the south channel bridge or if you expropriated the south channel bridge and gave the company rights over Pollys Gut bridge, the question arises as to what are you to do with the existing highway over Cornwall island. Generally speaking, you

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, under clause 7 there is a question of principle which disturbs me considerably. I am quite sure that the minister is not going to be prepared to do anything about it because he may be able to find some precedent for it in the past, but I think it is something to which we here in the house might very well take strong exception. I am referring to the matter of giving the St. Lawrence seaway authority the power, with the approval of the governor in council, to procure the incorporation of other corporations


for the purpose of carrying out its work. The renumbered clause which covers that will be 24 (a) (1).
I have always felt, and I think many hon. members in this house have also felt, that the further removed government bureaucracy and government administrative processes become from this house the more difficult they are to control, the more difficult they are to know anything about and the more opportunity there is for evasion of the proper authority and supervision by this house.
We have crown corporations at the present time which were set up in war time, and perhaps at that time they served a very necessary purpose; but carried on into peace time, we never see or hear and we never have a genuine chance to get at the details of the administration of these individual corporations. The one exception I can think of offhand, and it does not fall into quite the same class as the others, is the Canadian National Railways. The examination which its accounts receive in the committee on government-owned railways and shipping each year is, I think, beneficial to the company and it is illuminating to this house and to the representatives of this house who sit on the committee.
We have here a seaway authority which will be perhaps somewhat the same as the national harbours board. There is an opportunity in the estimates each year to have a look at the national harbours board and to comment on its operation. I would assume that there will be a similar opportunity in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway. But when the St. Lawrence seaway authority begins to incorporate subsidiary corporations to carry out its activities we reach the point at which this house will then be quite incapable of controlling its activities and it will be difficult for the house to know anything about it.
As I have said, I do not expect that as a result of these words or as a result of my pointing out this particular situation I am going to be able to shake the government in its present course, but I do think that legislation of this kind should not be allowed to pass without having it pointed out again and again and again that the government by means of legislation such as this and by means of other activities is taking the genuine power of examination and the power of control further and further away from the hands of this house year by year.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE OPERATION OF BRIDGES, ESTABLISHMENT OF TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to quote a paragraph from Hansard relating to this discussion. The paragraph is found

on page 3216 of Hansard of April 24, 1956 and it reads as follows:
This raises a question as to whether or not the tolls which would be charged for the use of this bridge would be kept entirely separate from the seaway tolls. It seems to me they have no relationship to the tolls which would be charged for the use of the canal. In one case the users of the bridge would pay their tolls and pay the cost of maintenance and ultimately the cost of building the bridge, and separate accounts should be kept. In the other case the users of the canal, or the shippers would pay their toll for shipping facilities. I am just pointing this out; doubtless these things have received consideration not only by the minister but by the seaway authority.
Those words were not mine. They were the words of the hon. member for St. Paul's. I think they were very sensible words and I am surprised that his colleague the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace does not share his opinion. Because I have been in opposition for a large part of my life, I suggest that one of the first things that is good for an opposition is to have them all speaking with the same voice. However, I am not trying to give the hon. member for St. Paul's any lesson. What he has said here in what I have just quoted makes sense. It is merely because it is the sound, common-sense approach to separating seaway tolls and seaway revenues from the possible revenues that may accrue from the operation of a highway bridge that the desirability of having the power to create a subsidiary is so manifest.
The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace fears that by this process the facts will be lost sight of. Mr. Chairman, I hope the facts will not be lost sight of. So far as the seaway corporation is concerned, I feel perfectly sure that when the seaway is completed, when it is in operation, all of the facts will be given to parliament because there will be nothing to hide and nothing that anybody will want to hide. I think that if one will consider these questions in a purely objective fashion, in the way in which the hon. member for St. Paul's considered them, we would all agree that it was desirable to have a subsidiary so as to maintain a desirable separation between the greatly differing activities.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AMENDMENTS TO AUTHORIZE OPERATION OF BRIDGES, ESTABLISHMENT OF TOLLS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would not want the remarks of the minister to go without an adequate reply because I think that, baldly stated as they were, they give quite a wrong impression. The minister, who has previous experience in opposition in other parts of this country and who also has extensive experience as a lawyer or a notary, must also know that there are many ways of keeping money separate and distinct, and of keeping funds
2,	1956	3491
St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act separate besides the necessity of making a special incorporation or incorporating a special company for the purpose. We need only to turn to the accounts of the federal government itself where we find that it is possible to have accounts for receipts and expenditures in a department, on a departmental basis, without the necessity of incorporating a special corporation. In a company with a number of varying operations one often finds that it will prepare separate financial statements and accounts for its returns without setting up one corporation per department.
I can see where the minister might like that. Just consider what would happen. The lawyers and the notaries of this country would be worked to death if you had to set up a separate corporation every time you wanted to make a separate accounting of your receipts. It seems to me that that is the basis of the argument that he has advanced. The only reason he has given us in this case was that, quite properly, it was necessary to keep the financial operations, the accounting for this bridge, separate from the other operations of the seaway. I do not see for a moment where that puts the hon. member for St. Paul's, who has the same fundamental idea, and me at odds, because we agree-in fact, surprisingly enough all three of us seem to agree-that the accounting for the operation of this bridge should be on a separate basis. Where I part company primarily with the minister is on the question of whether or not he needs to have the power to set up separate incorporations in order to deal with these particular problems. In that respect, it is my contention that he does not need that power.

the second reading of Bill No. 248, respecting the construction of a line of railway in the province of New Brunswick by Canadian National Railway Company from a point at or near Bartibog in a westerly direction to the Tomogonops river in the vicinity of Little River lakes.
He said: I explained the other day when the resolution was before the committee that the proposed branch line would commence at a point at or near Bartibog on the main line of the Canadian National Railways between Newcastle and Bathurst, in the province of New Brunswick, and would run in a westerly direction to the Tomogonops river in the vicinity of Little River lakes, a distance of approximately 22 miles. I also said that the estimate cost of the construction of the proposed line is $127,270 per mile or a total of about $2,800,000.
I also explained that Heath Steele Mines Limited, a subsidiary of American Metals Company, has expended large sums in proving up a substantial body of lead, zinc and copper ore and is at present actively engaged in readying the mine for production, including the installation of a concentrate mill at a capacity of 1,500 tons of ore daily. This company has requested the Canadian National Railways to construct the said branch line.
I gave some information with regard to the prospective volume of traffic and I told the members of the committee that it was contemplated that a traffic agreement would be entered into between Heath Steele Mines Limited and the railway company which would guarantee adequate traffic. I think
Canadian National Railways the figure I mentioned was 75,000 tons in any year. Under the contemplated traffic agreement there would be a penalty if in any year the volume of tonnage delivered to the railway by the company were less than 75,000 tons. I also explained that this was to be on a cumulative basis and, if the penalties were paid in one year but there were excess tonnage carried in a following year, the company would be entitled to be rebated the amount of any such penalties, the over-all intention being that during the six-year period an aggregate of 450,000 tons of concentrates could be carried by the railways.
I also pointed out that it was expected that this would enable the cutting of approximately 12,000 cords of pulpwood annually, and it was believed that with the freight in prospect, which I have already mentioned, and the other freight that would naturally develop, the branch line would be self-sustaining and would actually contribute something to the finances of the system as a whole.
The other day, several hon. members spoke on the resolution and commended its purpose. I hope that the bill itself will be received in the same spirit by the members of the house and that we may have it adopted and go ahead with the work as soon as possible. I should like to add just this further word, that the Canadian National Railways itself is most anxious to make a start with the work at as early a date as possible because, as will appear from the bill itself, the work is to be completed prior to November 1, 1958, and I understand they are anxious to get on with it so as to meet the date I have just mentioned.

I am sure this measure is being carried out in conjunction with the vast growing mining developments in northern New Brunswick. The expenditure of $2,800,000, part of which will be in my constituency of Gloucester, together with the anticipated annual cut of 12,000 cords of pulpwood per year, will provide additional employment in the area and will add to the federal government's contribution towards the development of New Brunswick's natural resources.
The mineral discoveries in the northern regions of New Brunswick will provide millions of tons of ore which will have to be extracted and transported to shipping points. We cannot disregard the advantages offered by the proximity of these mines to deep water harbours where shipping can take place twelve months in the year. Right in the vicinity of Bathurst, within a distance of 20 or 30 miles from the mineral deposits, we have a deep water harbour and a sufficient source of fresh water supply to permit the construction and operation of a smelter in order to refine within the province our rich deposits of zinc, lead, copper and silver. Forty miles farther away we also have at Pokesudi one of the best natural harbours on the Atlantic coast. There shipping can also take place 12 months in the year in sheltered water with a depth running from 27 to 30 feet within a few hundred feet from the shore.
With the discovery and development of these extensive base metal deposits, co-operation and even financial assistance for the procurement of a large and steady source of power will likely be required from the federal government. In addition to the provision of transportation facilities, these new and growing industrial centres will also require a constant supply of electrical energy for the electrochemical processing of their minerals. I am confident that the matter will receive favourable consideration if and when a definite request and proposal is presented to the government in this regard. When in the very near future other mining interests such as Brunswick Mining and Smelting, Anacon and others apply for additional spur lines to connect their mines and operations with the main line of the Canadian National, I am confident that similar favourable consideration will be given by the government and by Canadian National Railways.

Having said that, and without any desire to recapitulate what was said on an earlier occasion, I do wish to point out just one or two matters connected with the regulations which, in consequence of this amendment, will be continued in effect until May 31, 1958.
The regulations provide for a transport controller having authority to order any person dealing in various bulk commodities to fix minimum quotas, to fix proportions and the like and also to order any person dealing in bulk transport facilities, which include rail-1 ways, steamships and the like, to extend,


[furnish, supply or make use of any bulk transport facilities for transporting any bulk commodities. These powers are very wide. The transport controller becomes almost, if not completely, omnipotent. His authority is above the law; his discretion is unchallenge-jjJjle. I mention those powers because the results in the western provinces in so far as wheat transport is concerned have been ineffectual. Regulations, while artistic as window dressing, are ineffectual when they are not carried out. The enforcement of the regulations, the implementation of the powers has all the innocuity of eyewash. The powers are there. They have not been used. I make no personal criticism of Mr. Roy Milner. There are some who criticize him because of the fact that in an earlier day he held the presidency of the Winnipeg grain exchange, according to the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden), and was also one of the executive officials of one of the line grain companies. Those suggestions do nothing to meet the problem we face.
Sometimes I wonder whether the transport controller was set up for the purpose of acting as a scapegoat for the failure of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, first to provide markets for western wheat, and, second, to endeavour to delude the western farmer into believing that the reason that 97 per cent of western marketing points are on a 2-bushel or less quota is that there is a shortage of box cars. That would leave the inference that the responsibility for failure to maintain markets is not the government's but the transport controller's because of his failure to supply cars. The transport controller said as recently as February 17:
There is no shortage of box cars which have the effect of holding up prairie grain shipments.
Well, sir, if there was no shortage of box cars, then it is difficult to understand why some 90 million to 100 million bushels of available storage space remained vacant and unoccupied during the fall of last year when the western farmer found himself so short of money because of his inability to market at the 2,000 or more marketing places in the western provinces.
This was the position of the farmer. He had the wheat. It was not climatic conditions. That alibi is totally ineffectual. It was the fact that there were no markets available at the various marketing points, which denied the farmers of western Canada the opportunity to use at least 75 per cent of the 100 million bushels of available space.

loadings had recently increased to about MHO per day in the west, but more than 1,400 daily were needed to equal the loadings in the preceding crop year, Mr. Hansen said. I make this appeal to the minister; statistics are not helping the western farmer to market his wheat.
Mr. Hansen enjoys the trust of this government. He returned only recently from the meeting of the international wheat agreement conference which he attended as one

Department of Transport Act of the representatives of Canada and as recently as April 25, in the interview to which I have made reference, he set out the seriousness of the situation.
Again I repeat that when only 2 per cent of the western marketing points are on a 5-bushel quota something is very wrong or the 5-bushel quota would have been increased if there had been available cars to empty the various elevators in the local marketing places.
However one wishes to look at this matter, and however repetitious the claims on the part of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) have been that all is well, the fact remains that the situation is a serious one. Mr. Milner says it is not his responsibility. He has had the cars. I then ask, whose responsibility is it for what has had all the appearances of being energetic somnolence in the face of a serious situation amongst the western farmers?
There are three points, sir, that I wish to bring to the minister's attention. One is the need of removing the discriminatory shortages of box cars in certain marketing points. There has been gross ineffectiveness in the allocation and authorization of cars to the various marketing points. Equalize them. To equalize them I suggest that the rule that has heretofore existed that wheat grown on Canadian Pacific Railway lines shall not be diverted or stored in the Hudson bay facilities at Churchill be done away with, and that in so far as northern Saskatchewan and Manitoba are concerned, adjacent as these areas are to the Hudson bay storage facilities, those storage facilities should be made available to wheat grown on Canadian Pacific Railway lines.
Second, there should be a conference convened of representatives of organized agriculture, including two or three representatives of the various farm organizations, to meet with the railways to the end that the unfairnesses and discriminatory practices against certain marketing places be removed.
Third, in providing freight cars for the transport of wheat, those areas which have the low quotas of one or two bushels to the acre should be given an immediate preference.
How anyone can argue that somebody has not slipped up is quite beyond me when I point out the fact, which I now repeat, that at only 2 per cent of all the marketing points in western Canada has the farmer a 5-bushel quota.
What does that mean? A 5-bushel quota will not pay his expenses. Yet in only 2 per cent of the cases do the farmers have that


quota. In approximately 7 per cent of the marketing places the farmer has a quota of only one or two bushels per acre. In other words, he receives about $2.50 per acre. That is all he has been able to realize. There seems to be nothing to rectify what is quite evidently the basis of discrimination. I should like to know from the minister whether, if that discrimination is pointed out to him or his transport controller, he will take steps to see that it is corrected.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext: I suggest that if the hon. member has a specific case he bring it to my attention and I shall investigate it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext: I shall be pleased to do that. Shall I call it six o'clock?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
I should like to point out to the minister that I have in my hand a letter written on February 22 and signed by the transport controller in which he makes this statement:
The allocation of cars to stations or to elevator companies at a station is entirely under the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board.
I have other correspondence here, Mr. Chairman, which points out that certain elevator agents did have shipping orders from the wheat board but were unable to obtain cars. The transport controller tells us it is not his business and the minister says it is his business.

speechtext: I said he had the power to do it, but I did not say it was his responsibility.
